endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Verify that configuration change control processes are established and in place [4], [5]. Determine whether the organization formally records and stores changes to the AI solution’s deployment environment.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Device Software Functions: Lifecycle Management and Marketing Submission Recommendations (draft guidance)
endorsements.quote: A description of the data recording mechanisms that will be used to record the 1210 version or state of the AI-enabled device used during the study for a given 1211 patient.

endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: AI incident reports should reference the model version and data vintage active at the time of the incident to enable traceability.

endorsements.title: Model centric collaboration reduces data sharing barriers in medical artificial intelligence
endorsements.quote: Third, trust mechanisms for model exchange must be established, including versioning, provenance tracking, and validation benchmarks, so that institutions can assess the reliability and scope of externally derived model components before integration into local systems.

endorsements.title: Co-Lifecycle Governance for Learning Medical AI: A Hybrid Convergence Framework for Adaptive Regulatory Oversight
endorsements.quote: Co-Lifecycle Governance therefore emphasizes traceability: a chain of custody for model versions, validation evidence, deployment context, and corrective actions, which supports both clinical trust and legal enforceability [ 25-28 ].

endorsements.title: A five-phase evaluation framework for diagnostic and predictive medical artificial intelligence
endorsements.quote: Regardless of the specific approach, the phase must ensure that AI versions, thresholds, and interfaces remain stable and traceable throughout the study; that failure modes and anomalous events arising in real workflows are systematically documented; that performance consistency is monitored across institutions, devices, and patient groups; and that comprehensive records of data governance, privacy protection, and model‑update processes are maintained.

endorsements.title: Lifecycle answerability for artificial intelligence-enabled medical device software: a regulatory science perspective
endorsements.quote: Uncertainty records, dissent capture, versioned decision trails, local validation thresholds, and revalidation pathways should be treated as linked parts of lifecycle control, so that a clinical concern can change what is monitored, validated, updated, or retired.

evidence.title: Adaptive FHIR Native AI Governance for Clinical Decision Support: A Modular, Auditable Deployment Framework for Real World Clinical AI
evidence.outcome: Traceability of selected model per decision via Provenance resources
evidence.effect: Framework emitted Provenance and AuditEvent capturing selected model and decision timing; 100% deterministic reconstruction of deployment pathways in simulation.
evidence.quote: All deployment decisions generated complete HL7 FHIR AuditEvent and Provenance artifacts, enabling 100% deterministic reconstruction of deployment pathways.

evidence.title: Testing the Black Box: Structural Barriers to Independent Evaluation of Consumer-Facing Health LLMs
evidence.outcome: Traceability of consumer LLM model versions for replication
evidence.effect: Models changed without traceable version identifiers, preventing reliable replication of evaluations.
evidence.quote: Models changed without traceable version identifiers, preventing reliable replication.

evidence.title: A Clinical Quality-Assurance Panel for Patient-Facing Black-Box Large Language Models in Healthcare: Anchored Forced-Choice Drift Monitoring for Sensitive Communication
evidence.effect: No stable build identifier beyond product label; temperature and seed not controllable.
evidence.quote: The interface did not expose a stable build identifier beyond the product label, and temperature and random seed were not user-controllable.

commentary.bottom_line: One simulation study found that a framework recording the selected model with each decision allowed 100% deterministic reconstruction of 2,272 simulated deployment decisions, and no study has tested version traceability in live clinical use or linked it to patient outcomes. Seven sources endorse the practice, one study found that untraceable version changes prevented reliable replication of evaluations, and a second found no stable build identifier beyond a product label.

perspectives.view: The only test of the practice is a single level 4 simulation of 2,272 sequential deployment decisions, with no clinical setting or patients. It reports full reconstruction of deployment pathways, an outcome that is indirect to harm tracing in care. With one study and no replication, certainty is very low.

Two studies show the failure mode exists. Consumer model versions changed without identifiers, and one product exposed no stable build identifier and no control of temperature or seed. The simulation suggests provenance logging can record which model made each decision, but it did not test whether that record helps investigators find the cause of a real incident.

The tested framework wrote Provenance and AuditEvent resources capturing the selected model and decision timing. This suggests version logging can be built on standard interoperability resources. The study ran offline, so it gives no information on logging fidelity, storage burden, or behavior when vendors update models without notice.

FDA draft guidance asks sponsors to describe how they will record the device version or state used for each study patient, and CHAI frameworks ask for change control and version references in incident reports. One benchmark found no stable build identifier beyond a product label, which may leave implementers unable to meet these expectations without contract terms requiring build identifiers.

The benchmark that found no stable build identifier included limited English proficiency or non-English trials, which suggests the tracing problem may extend to evaluations for those users. That study documents the problem only. The simulation that tested traceability did not report its population and offers no evidence on whether the practice works equally across patient groups.

commentary.research_gap: No study has tested model version traceability in a live clinical deployment, measured whether it shortens or improves incident investigation, or estimated its cost and data storage burden. Studies comparing incident root-cause analysis with and without version and data-vintage logging, including cases where vendors update models silently, would address the main uncertainty.
commentary.underserved_note: The one test of the practice was a simulation with no reported population, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. One hazard benchmark involved non-English trials and found no stable build identifier, which suggests the problem may reach these groups, but whether the practice helps them remains untested.
